public_rationale: His hedged claim was that SoftBank would need significant new debt or sales of valuable stakes to meet its OpenAI-era commitments. That is how it paid. SoftBank's November 2025 earnings disclosure showed it sold its entire Nvidia stake for $5.83 billion and T-Mobile shares for $9.17 billion, and used an Arm-backed margin loan to fund the OpenAI commitment. In February 2026 it disclosed $27 billion of new debt in Q4 2025 and further T-Mobile sales; that cash helped pay the $22.5 billion it sent to OpenAI in December. SoftBank's CFO called the borrowing conservative, but that does not change the fact that the money came from new debt and stake sales.
limitations: The evidence shows how SoftBank paid, not that it could not have paid any other way.

our_interpretation: He hedged ('based on my analysis', 'does not appear'). We do not treat this as a claim that SoftBank could not possibly have paid any other way. The plain reading is narrower: to meet these commitments, SoftBank would have to rely on significant new borrowing or on selling valuable stakes, not on cash it already had.

Whether SoftBank could have paid from existing cash cannot be observed directly. The best test is how SoftBank actually paid. If its own disclosures show it funded the OpenAI payments mainly with significant new debt or sales of valuable holdings, that supports the claim. If it paid from existing cash without material new debt or stake sales, that contradicts it.

Target period: 24 March 2025 (the post date) to 31 March 2026. This is the shortest payment schedule he cited for the OpenAI money ('12 to 24 months starting as soon as spring'). It covers the main OpenAI payments.
Commitments SoftBank made later (such as the further $30 billion OpenAI investment agreed in February 2026) are outside the commitments he described. They are context only.
criteria.support_condition: SoftBank disclosures, or reliable reports of them, show that it paid its 2025 OpenAI commitments with significant new borrowing (bridge loans, margin loans, bonds) and/or by selling valuable stakes in companies it held.
criteria.contradiction_condition: SoftBank paid these commitments mainly from cash it already had or from operating cash flow, without significant new debt or sales of valuable holdings.

evidence.excerpt: it took on an additional $27 billion in debt in the last three months of the year, including debt at its subsidiaries. It also sold over $3.5 billion in shares of T-Mobile, on top of the previously announced $5.8 billion it raised by selling a stake in Nvidia.

evidence.excerpt: SoftBank CFO Yoshimitsu Goto said Thursday the company's debt amounts to just 20% of the total value of SoftBank's assets -- a more conservative borrowing policy SoftBank developed after prior tech busts scared investors.
evidence.explanation: SoftBank's view that its borrowing stayed within a conservative loan-to-value limit. This speaks to whether the debt was risky, not to whether new debt and stake sales were needed.
